items.title: Des structures de santé entre paralysie et continuité
items.description: Le Syndicat autonome des médecins, pharmaciens et chirurgiens-dentistes du Sénégal (Sames) a entamé, ce mardi 8 septembre, son mouvement de grève de 48 heures avec respect des urgences. À l’Hôpital général Idrissa Pouye de Grand-Yoff (Dakar), la grève a été largement suivie. Par contre, le centre de santé Nabil Choucair de la Patte d’Oie n’a pas été impacté. L’Hôpital général Idrissa Pouye de Grand-Yoff, une des structures sanitaires de référence de la région de Dakar, a présenté un autre visage, hier, mardi 8 septembre, avec la grève du Syndicat autonome des médecins, pharmaciens et chirurgiens-dentistes du Sénégal (Sames). Devant l’établissement, un parking de véhicules fait face aux portes d’entrée. Deux entrées distinctes permettent d’accéder à l’hôpital sous le contrôle de vigiles. Devant le secrétariat médical, deux femmes sont installées derrière les vitres du bâtiment des consultations externes. Elles s’occupent de l’accueil et de l’orientation des patients. Elles nous ont fait savoir que les médecins ne sont pas venus ce matin (hier). L'une d’elles déclare : « Les médecins sont en grève. Seules les urgences sont assurées ». Les rares personnes qui circulent dans cette partie de l’hôpital ont plié bagage. Assis encore sous un arbre, un sachet à la main, Ibrahima Diallo espère toujours être reçu par un praticien. Vêtu d’une djellaba toute blanche assortie d’un bonnet jaune, il est venu de la Guinée-Bissau pour se faire soigner au Sénégal. Après plusieurs jours passés à l’hôpital général de Grand-Yoff, pour une prise en charge médicale, il devait avoir l’aval du médecin pour rentrer chez lui. Mais, la grève a bouleversé son programme. Il avoue avoir été renvoyé à vendredi prochain, faute de médecin. Devant la salle des consultations externes, une autre patiente semble désemparée. De forte corpulence, elle porte un vêtement en wax aux couleurs vives. Venue de Diass, dans la région de Thiès, elle préfère garder l’anonymat. Elle raconte avoir pris un taxi sans savoir que les médecins sont en grève. Ce n’est qu’une fois sur place qu’elle découvre que les consultations sont à l'arrêt. Après un long trajet, elle se retrouve bloquée sans pouvoir se faire soigner. Si la majorité des services sont paralysés par la grève, ceux réservés à l’accueil et aux urgences fonctionnent. L’écriteau « Service d’accueil et d’urgence », inscrit en grosses lettres rouges, est bien visible. Des patients de tous âges et aux profils variés attendent devant les salles. Visiblement éprouvés, patients et accompagnateurs sont à la cherche de médecins. Dans ce service, les activités médicales sont au ralenti avec un service minimum. Les usagers se contentent de cela. Après Grand-Yoff, cap sur le centre de santé Nabil Choucair à la Patte D’Oie. À l’intérieur de la structure, on constate une nette affluence. Devant les salles de consultation et la pédiatrie, les usagers sont nombreux : certains sont assis, d’autres debout. Les ventilateurs tournent sans relâche et apportent un léger réconfort malgré la forte canicule. De temps à autre, des discussions s’élèvent autour de l'ordre d’arrivée et de passage. Chacun tient scrupuleusement son ticket. Les agents de santé sont bien visibles dans les couloirs. Ils entrent et sortent des bureaux. L’activité se poursuit au sein de la structure sanitaire.Abou Diallo, un patient, cherche un chemin. Il est venu faire un contrôle de glycémie. Il a été pris en charge. À quelques pas, un homme attend son tour, affirmant ne pas être au courant de la grève des médecins. Dans la salle portant la mention « Médecin 2 », un patient vient de sortir. Un praticien de teint clair, des lunettes transparentes ajustées sur le nez, est penché sur son registre, occupé à consigner les dossiers. Interrogé sur la grève, il précise qu’il n’est pas membre du Sames. Un patient sous l’anonymat abonde dans le même sens, puisque n’étant pas au courant de la grève. Ameth NIASS (Stagiaire)

items.title: This Was a Good Sculpture
items.description: Until last week, a big electric-blue sculpture by Joel Shapiro sat next to the Kennedy Center. Boxy and rigid but seemingly weightless, Blue looked like a clumsy person who’d been swept by a breeze into an accidental pirouette. Shapiro called the metalwork a “celebration of possibility.” Some people thought it looked like Gumby. I loved it. The leaders of the Kennedy Center—and there is really just one leader of the Kennedy Center—did not. Workers dismantled Blue last Wednesday. No specific reason was given, save that the change had occurred at the center’s request. Internal documents obtained by The New York Times say that the sculpture was targeted for removal soon after Donald Trump took control of the institution. Shapiro—one of the most important American sculptors of his generation—died last summer. He spent decades coaxing human gesture and emotion from the austere geometry of minimalism. His abstract shapes and forms have strong personalities. They lie in wait for their audience, then suddenly come alive. I knew Shapiro a little, through his wife, the artist Ellen Phelan. He was owlish, warm, blunt, and inspiring to be around, always searching for what he called a “little moment of rapture.” Blue was one of those. It wasn’t gilded. Shapiro spent two years in India in the Peace Corps, which President John F. Kennedy established. The antecedent for the Kennedy Center was right there in New Delhi: the architect Edward Durell Stone’s striking new American embassy, which he would channel in his later design for a national arts center—which would be named for Kennedy after his assassination. Decades later, Shapiro made monumental works for American diplomatic missions overseas. Blue , fittingly, stood near the Kennedy Center’s Peace Corps Gallery. Washington, D.C.’s landscape is full of these cords of connection—some accidental, some carefully arranged. This one was simply cut, leaving a blemish in a city full of symbols. Those symbols are everywhere. You can walk from the Kennedy Center to the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum in a brisk half hour. I’ve taken this route frequently, usually while running. The parks, the monuments, the cherry trees, and the limestone edifices of federal power all prompt questions: about who gets memorialized, what myths and whose money might explain why, and who’s missing. One reason I repeat this route so often is to keep an inventory. What moved? What vanished? What’s next? Some landmarks—the State Department, in Foggy Bottom, for instance—haven’t changed but were hollowed by the Trump administration’s personnel cuts. The Lincoln Memorial is no longer visible in the botched Reflection Pool, an eyesore that’s been drained again to fix a shoddy renovation. [ Read: The Kennedy Center has a problem that courts can’t fix ] Keep going, past the memorials to World War II and the Korean War, and, nearby, Maya Lin’s black-granite scar, elegizing U.S. troops in Vietnam. I love odd and nerdy things along this route: statues of 19th-century Latin American liberators, Cold War allegorical bronzes, and, tucked away, Robert Berks’s playful Einstein. (People like to sit on his lap and rub his nose.) Einstein said, “Force always attracts men of low morality.” Another cord of connection: Berks made the giant bronze bust of Kennedy that resides inside the Kennedy Center. Push farther, past the Jefferson Memorial and the Tidal Basin, until Independence Avenue and the Holocaust Museum—which had its own upheaval last year, when Trump purged its board of trustees—come into view. Here, less than two miles from the Kennedy Center, stands another big Joel Shapiro—his portentously titled Loss and Regeneration . It’s one of his most painful, deeply moving works. Two black-bronze forms: a windowless house crashed upside down on its roof and, 100 feet away, an unstable but determined tree-like shape. Life after genocide. The house is inscribed with lines translated from a poem by an unnamed child in the Terezín ghetto: Until, after a long, long time, I’d be well again. Then I’d like to live And go back home again. I’ve memorized those words. Shapiro made this work in 1993. Blue arrived at the Kennedy Center in 2019, a gift from the artist and a centerpiece of the REACH, the campus’s elegant expansion that brought more art and more audiences. Blue and Loss became the cardinal points of my run: possibility and devastation. I doubt anyone else did this, but I got in the habit of tap-touching them: Blue at the start. Loss before I headed home. President Dwight Eisenhower authorized the creation of a national cultural center in Washington, D.C. But Kennedy worked hard to bring it into existence. Almost two years into his presidency, he gave a nationally televised speech to launch a public campaign for it—with appearances by Marian Anderson, Leonard Bernstein, Robert Frost, Harry Belafonte, and a 7-year-old Yo-Yo Ma. Kennedy spoke that night about art being political “in the most profound sense, not as a weapon in the struggle but as an instrument of understanding” among humanity. That was a perfect fit for Shapiro. I love how he could weld whimsy and catastrophe: a big blue dancer a short walk from an overturned house and a dark tree. But he also said that his sculptures have an “obdurate” sense of self. Blue will carry that obdurate spirit with it—down the National Mall to the National Gallery of Art. David Rubenstein, the chairman of the museum’s board and the former chairman of the Kennedy Center (he was ousted by Trump), just bought it from Shapiro’s foundation. That walk from whimsy to catastrophe just got shorter. Blue has a new home. I need a new path.

items.title: What September 11 Took From Me
items.description: During a visit in May to the Maritime Museum in Halifax, Nova Scotia, I watched a film about a 1917 cargo-ship explosion that killed more than 1,700 townspeople and injured many more. The grainy black-and-white images of the flattened city catapulted me back to the devastation of Lower Manhattan after terrorists attacked the World Trade Center on September 11, 2001. Halifax suffered a blizzard following the cargo-ship catastrophe, and the sight of the city covered in a deep blanket of snow recalled the dust and debris from the once-glimmering towers that coated the Financial District. When I heard the recorded voices of the Haligonian survivors recounting their memories, I walked out of the small theater to cry. Twenty-five years on from September 11, 2001, an image or memory can still evoke the very moment I learned that my 36-year-old redheaded husband, Jeffrey R. Smith, would not be coming home from work that day. Sasha Arutyunova for The Atlantic I, too, am now a voice in a museum. At the National September 11 Memorial & Museum, any visitor can replay my family’s intensely personal memories of a national horror. Years before the museum had a building, curators teamed up with StoryCorps, an oral-history nonprofit, and tried to make it easy for families to contribute by giving us a special number to call and record from home. Making this call felt like a leap of faith. How would these recordings be used? Where would they be stored? Still, my two daughters—who were then 8 and 10 years old—and I decided we wanted to participate. [ Ellen S. Bakalian: Everything my husband wasn’t there for ] I remember sitting on the couch while the girls took turns, cupping their hands over my cellphone in a semblance of privacy. I also recall one of them wandering the house, chatting like a teenager. I remember wanting them to practice what they would say, and I wanted to hear it before they called, but my girls had their own ideas. I found it nerve-racking until I realized that whatever they said would be straight from the hearts of girls who were not yet 3 and not yet 1 when their father was killed. I haven't heard the recordings. I recently thought that I wanted to, but I couldn't imagine donning headphones and listening to my voice or my daughters’ amid strangers at the museum. I contacted the chief curator, who kindly offered a private place for me to revisit what we had said. I made a date, then canceled it. I doubt I will reschedule. I know that if I listened, the editor in me would wish we could rerecord, and the rest of me would fall apart. Sasha Arutyunova for The Atlantic When we were in Nova Scotia, my friends and I took turns reading historical plaques out loud. I always make a point of reading the names on memorials wherever I find them. Years ago, one Presidents’ Day weekend, my daughters and I took the train to Washington, D.C. I remember standing in front of the Vietnam Veterans Memorial and deciding that we would read one young soldier’s name aloud as we traced our fingers over the letters. We looked up a 19-year-old soldier on a sheaf of laminated paper that was hanging on the wall and read the name of his hometown. We said a prayer for him and his family because, as I remember explaining to the girls, “one day Daddy’s name will be on a plaque somewhere, and we want people to read his name out loud.” The name Jeffrey R. Smith can be found by museumgoers in Lower Manhattan, and is also on two plaques at the University of Rochester, where Jeff earned both his undergraduate and master’s degrees. I went with my daughters to see these tributes when the girls were 18 and 16. We walked in Jeff’s footsteps. We read all of the names out loud. Unlike the men and women whose names appear on the Vietnam memorial, Jeff and the thousands of other innocent victims that Tuesday morning were not casualties of war. This is an important distinction, a line that I, like most September 11 widows and widowers, believe should not be blurred. America was senselessly and successfully attacked by terrorists, and Jeff, along with nearly 3,000 other civilians, was killed while going about an otherwise ordinary day. [ From the September 2026 issue: The man who refused to sit on the sidelines ] Knowing that our voices are in a museum because our profound personal loss is part of this country’s history is both gratifying and unsettling. I am glad that there is such a powerful monument to that awful day. I am grateful that my husband and the other innocent victims are commemorated each year with a moment of silence. But I am staggered to be part of something this big, forever and ever. Sasha Arutyunova for The Atlantic On this anniversary, I think of the couples who get to experience such milestones differently—joyfully, gratefully, together. Jeff and I will never have that. This is the pain that lurks just below the surface, only to bubble up without warning, like in a museum in Halifax. I know, of course, that I am one story, one tragedy, among many. But within our national catastrophe, which changed so much about our collective understanding of security, of terror, is my own private and persistent grief.

items.title: The Wild West of Commercial Surrogacy
items.description: Illustrations by Molly Snee When Shoshannah Roberts talks about the four babies she’s given away, she glows. “When I think about it now, it still feels emotional,” she told me. “Those moments are so magical.” For many women, the thought of handing over a newborn to someone else is almost incomprehensible—they feel a deep revulsion at a primal sundering. But for Roberts, acting as a surrogate four times is the most meaningful thing she has done with her life. “I’ve seen the parents hold their babies right away, skin to skin. I mean, like, raw ,” she said. “Baby’s off me, cord is cut, and Mom is just holding her baby and sobbing. It’s amazing.” The first time I saw Roberts, who lives in Santa Barbara County, California, she was speaking at the Men Having Babies conference in downtown San Francisco. Men Having Babies does exactly what its name promises: The organization helps gay aspiring fathers find women who are willing—eager, even—to carry their children. For one weekend every year, more than 200 men from across California and beyond fill the ballroom at the Marines’ Memorial Club & Hotel and listen to panel discussions and keynotes, with a special breakout session for single dads. Since the legalization of same-sex marriage, male couples have become the big growth market for American surrogacy, but the practice is booming among aspiring parents—married or single, straight or gay—who can afford the cost of hiring someone else to carry their child. In 2024, 11,821 embryos were transferred to surrogates in American clinics associated with the Society for Assisted Reproductive Technology, up from 8,461 three years earlier, and the United Nations estimates that the global worth of the industry is almost $15 billion. Most surrogacy in America today is commercial, meaning that the carrier is paid, and gestational, meaning that the carrier has no genetic relationship to the child. Marissa Leshnov for The Atlantic Shoshannah Roberts, photo­graphed in Los Angeles, is pregnant with her fifth child. She has carried four more babies as a surrogate. Barely a week passes without another celebrity posing with their new baby on Instagram—perhaps in scrubs or doing skin-to-skin contact—and thanking their heroic surrogate. Kim Kardashian, Anderson Cooper, Meghan Trainor, and Chrissy Teigen have all used surrogates. Some celebrities, citing medical risks, hire a surrogate to take on the dangers of pregnancy for them. Others want more children than they can have biologically. Hilaria and Alec Baldwin had a sixth baby via surrogate five months after Hilaria gave birth to their fifth child. (She has since carried their seventh.) But just as paid surrogacy is becoming a more conspicuous part of American life, so, too, is the backlash. When the actor Lily Collins, then 35, announced the birth of her baby, Tove, and her “endless gratitude for our incredible surrogate,” she and her husband were bombarded with messages describing them as “human traffickers” and “baby buyers.” In the past year, multiple horror stories—fraudulent agencies, human trafficking, elderly parents who are unable to take care of a newborn—have emerged, complicating what is usually presented as an uplifting narrative. If your primary concern is reproductive freedom, most surrogacy stories will seem inspirational. But if you factor in the risks to carriers, or simply feel skeptical of unregulated commerce, your doubts will multiply. In my experience, many liberal Americans are surprised to discover that their country is an outlier in its enthusiasm for commercial surrogacy. In Britain, where I live, a ban on the practice enjoys substantial support among feminists, who worry about the power differential between paid surrogates and wealthy would-be parents. (Altruistic surrogacy, in which the surrogate carries a baby solely out of generosity, is less controversial and is permitted.) A recent UN report went even further , declaring that commercial surrogacy “constitutes the sale of children, which is a crime,” and that “surrogacy arrangements can amount to or resemble slavery.” In one recent scandal, Thai women who answered an advertisement for work as surrogates in the nation of Georgia had their passports confiscated and were coerced into donating their eggs . Several developing countries that have become hubs for surrogacy tourism have enacted laws to protect women from exploitation by wealthy foreigners. Thailand banned commercial surrogacy in 2015 after the “ Baby Gammy ” case, in which a surrogate was left caring for a disabled child. She alleged that she had become pregnant with twins and refused a request by the intended parents—one of whom was a convicted sex offender—to abort the twin with Down syndrome. Because so much can go wrong, every country in the European Union has banned commercial surrogacy. France’s centrist liberal president, Emmanuel Macron, has described the practice as “not compatible with the dignity of women.” Italy’s right-wing populist leader, Giorgia Meloni, has enacted one of the strictest anti-surrogacy frameworks in the world. Not only is domestic surrogacy banned, but any Italian citizen who brings home a baby born to an overseas surrogate risks jail and a fine of up to 1 million euros. Many other developed countries have either tightly restricted surrogacy or chosen, as Britain and Canada have, to allow only the altruistic version. Israel allows surrogacy but imposes a raft of conditions: The commissioning parents must not have more than two children already, must not have serious criminal convictions, and must be of the same religion as the surrogate. In general, Europeans think of Americans’ enthusiasm for paid surrogacy the way we regard their fondness for guns and capital punishment: inexplicable. The piquant difference, however, is that surrogacy is a cause of the American left rather than the right. Red states tend to have tighter limits on surrogacy. Louisiana, for example, restricts surrogacy to married heterosexual couples using their own sperm and eggs. By contrast, when New York legalized commercial surrogacy in 2020, LGBTQ activists hailed it as a triumph for “fertility equality.” The debate cuts across political traditions and defies easy categorization. When surrogacy goes well, the result is a happy family that would not otherwise have existed. When it goes wrong, however, it can do so in unpredictable and emotionally crushing ways. At its core, the ethical question is this: How much physical and emotional risk should individuals be allowed to take on in the name of a commercial transaction? California, the home of Hollywood and Silicon Valley, is the undisputed center of American surrogacy, and the practice there is infused with a distinct blend of crunchy vibes, social liberalism, and straightforward capitalism. Surrogacy costs in the state begin at about $150,000 for a single baby, according to promotional materials for a variety of agencies doing business there. The percentage paid to the surrogate varies widely. Many, many enterprises want to help make gay couples’ dreams of parenthood come true, and the Men Having Babies conference was underwritten by a number of them: IVF clinics, genetic-testing companies, and surrogacy agencies. If the sea of Zegna sneakers and stylish down jackets didn’t tell you that these guys have money, the brochures offering future fathers “white-glove service” and VIP packages made it clear. In the exhibitors’ hall, I passed an abundance of merch designed to reel clients in—candles bearing the instruction LIGHT ME WHEN MATCHED , onesies with I LOVE MY DADS on them, canvas bags with the legend DADDY VIBES , and my own favorite: multiple iterations of sperm-shaped stress balls. Some were dyed rainbow colors. This was aspirational parenthood, right here. Pictures of happy dads and adorable kids abounded, including on a banner featuring two ripped, waxed, shirtless guys draped in a Pride flag and cradling a newborn. Words such as bespoke , boutique , and concierge appeared frequently in the literature. Words such as episiotomy and mastitis did not. It was here that I learned the industry’s preferred term for a surrogate pregnancy: a journey . At its best, surrogacy showers happiness all around. Intended parents—or IPs, in industry jargon—receive a longed-for baby; their surrogate is well compensated and well treated, and has the satisfaction of knowing that she has helped create a family. A few days after the conference, Roberts told me over Zoom that she had been interested in surrogacy ever since Phoebe on Friends carried triplets for her brother, Frank. Her first experience was blissful: She carried for a single mom who met a partner midway through the pregnancy, and Roberts later attended their beach wedding, in Florida. When she went back to work at a corporate job, “it felt a little hollow,” she said. She joined the surrogacy agency Hatch as a coordinator. In addition to four surrogate pregnancies, she’s had four children of her own. “My grandmother had 12,” she said. “So I think I’m built for it.” In mid-June, she announced her ninth pregnancy—another baby of her own. In the United States, the only serious opposition to surrogacy comes from an unlikely coalition of radical feminists and socially conservative Catholics. The former see surrogacy as exploitation: In 1983’s Right-Wing Women , the feminist author Andrea Dworkin described surrogacy as part of the “brothel model” of society, where “women can sell reproductive capacities the same way old-time prostitutes sold sexual ones.” Catholics, meanwhile, have doctrinal objections to any artificial interference in pregnancy. The more typical American view, though, tends toward individualism, in line with the “My body, my choice” slogan popularized by the abortion-rights movement, and an instinctive suspicion of government regulation: If the surrogate is okay with it, what business is it of anyone else? Although you can’t legally sell a kidney—even America has its limits—consent is treated as a universal solvent for many other tricky ethical issues. Well-heeled intended parents can also dodge practical constraints faced by biological or adoptive parents. Many agencies place no hard restrictions on the number of children any single person or couple can commission. Some parents want to get to a “double-digit number,” Men Having Babies’ founder, Ron Poole-Dayan, said at the conference. In 2023, a court in Los Angeles discovered that the Chinese video-game billionaire Xu Bo was simultaneously seeking parental rights for four babies born via surrogacy and was in the process of fathering at least eight more. The children (all boys, at his request) were being raised by nannies in nearby Irvine until they could be taken to him in China , The Wall Street Journal reported. There are also no legally enforceable upper age limits on intended parents. In August 2025, two 6-year-old children were found in a caged-off section of a San Francisco apartment. Their father explained that he had commissioned twins as a single dad at the age of 67, and when one of the babies was diagnosed with severe autism, he found himself struggling to cope. The locked gate stopped the neurodivergent twin from injuring himself during tantrums or running out of the building into the road. “I’m a senior, first-time parent, single parent, to twins, without domestic help,” the 74-year-old told The San Francisco Standard after he was reported to child services. (To which I might respond: And you didn’t think about this earlier? ) Difficulties like these are why many adoption agencies suggest an upper age limit of about 50. The surrogacy industry does not have a regulator that enforces a “fit and proper person” test of the kind given to people who want to adopt a child. Last year, Pennsylvania lawmakers proposed closing a loophole in the state’s law that had allowed a sex offender—who was legally barred from adopting or fostering—to commission a baby. There are no restrictions on Americans commissioning a baby abroad, even if the other country’s health services or human-rights laws are far worse than those in the United States. America also stands virtually alone as a rich country that permits incoming surrogacy tourism from elsewhere. Many of these international intended parents are from China , where surrogacy is banned and where, until recently, family size was limited by the one-child policy. These customers have exacting standards. “They want a Caucasian surrogate to carry the baby, with preferably blond hair, blue eyes,” Dee Gulati of Surrogacy4All, in New York, told me. “And they want an egg donor who looks like a cheerleader.” The resulting babies are automatically American citizens. (Hoping to change this, President Trump in August signed an executive order denying citizenship to children born to foreign citizens through commercial surrogacy.) In the U.S., no federal laws regulate surrogacy, and contracts related to the practice are unenforceable in many states. The Society for Ethics in Egg Donation and Surrogacy provides a “self-regulation framework” for agencies, but its greatest sanction is removing membership. The lack of regulation means that success depends more on luck and personal benevolence than on industry standards or legal guardrails. The primary question asked of parents attempting this new American way of birth is: Can you afford it? For some surrogates, handing over the baby is far harder than it was for Shoshannah Roberts. Last fall, in Chattanooga, Tennessee, I met Erika Jones, a quiet, self-contained woman who wore a discreet gold cross around her neck. She told me that her three ambitions in life had always been to visit Ireland, to be a surrogate, and to see a koala in person. She had wanted to be a surrogate since she was very young, before she’d even had her own two children. A few years ago, when she found herself settled in Fairfield, Ohio, with a good job and a stable income, she registered with an agency. The story of one couple particularly moved her. The wife, whom I’ll call Priya, had lost her brother to cancer in 2020. He’d banked his sperm before he died, and his family hoped to use it to fertilize a donor egg. The resulting embryo would then be carried by a surrogate and raised by Priya and her husband, allowing a part of her brother to live on. After Jones, then 34, learned the baby’s sex, she spent $40 on a balloon filled with pink confetti and had it sent to Priya, who recorded her reaction when she opened the box. But Jones didn’t see what she had hoped to see. “You could tell that she was disappointed that it was a girl,” Jones said. “I think she wanted a boy, to closely remind her of her brother.” Would the baby inside her be treated with respect, Jones wondered—or as second-best? From that point, in Jones’s telling, the relationship between the two women began to sour. Jones found Priya fussy and controlling, and felt that she was being blamed when a scan found that the fetus was growing unusually slowly. “I was like, I’m not a slave ,” she said. She even wondered briefly about trying to keep the baby, but decided that wouldn’t be right. When Jones found mold and detected carbon monoxide in her apartment, in Ohio, she decided to move back home to Tennessee, closer to her family. That would violate her 57-page “gestational carrier agreement,” in which she had agreed to “take all necessary and reasonable steps” to give birth at UC Health in West Chester, Ohio. The intended parents told her that if the baby was born in Tennessee, they would face “significant legal challenges.” Because of the state’s more restrictive laws, they feared, the contract might not be valid there. Priya and her husband suggested that Jones stay put and send her children to Tennessee to stay with a friend or relative for the remaining five months of the pregnancy. Jones declined. She moved back to Tennessee but agreed to keep traveling to Ohio for medical appointments and then give birth there. She was being paid $45,000 plus expenses for the pregnancy but found that the frequent back-and-forth between states, in addition to her time off work while sick, had eaten into that payment. She cut off direct contact with Priya and emailed the agency asking that she not attend the birth. “I know I signed the contract—I am well aware and I intend on honoring it,” Jones wrote, “but it does not need to continue to be thrown in my face every other day.” She also bought a puppy, aware that she would soon be coming home from the hospital empty-handed; she wanted, she later wrote in a memoir, something “alive, soft and ours.” Aileen Perilla for The Atlantic Erika Jones, photographed in Chattanooga, Tennessee. Jones had wanted to be a surrogate since she was very young. When Jones went into labor, she brought her two children, then ages 10 and 12, to the hospital, along with Susan Harris, a trusted friend, who alerted Priya and her husband. The labor was long—37 hours, 22 of them without an epidural. When Jones told the midwives that she wanted to push, the room suddenly filled with people. Earlier in her labor, Jones had asked for five minutes with the baby before handing her over. But the moment the little girl was delivered, she said, someone shouted, “No contact!” All she saw was a glimpse of dark-brown hair as the baby was taken away. She was not even told her birth weight. (Harris confirmed this account.) Priya told The Atlantic that she wasn’t “in any way disappointed” that the baby was a girl. She felt that because Jones had signed a legal contract agreeing to not have any skin-to-skin contact with the baby, she didn’t have to honor Jones’s request to hold her. “Maybe if you were nicer,” she thought. She has since ignored Jones’s request to talk through what happened. “At the end of the day, this is a business. We’re not friends,” she told The Atlantic . “You’re not doing me a favor. You’re getting paid $5,000 a month.” Both parties had fulfilled their side of the contract, she said, and it was time to move on. Jones has not found that so easy. She told me that the experience kept playing in her mind: “I felt like I was treated less than a human, and less than an animal.” According to the industry , unhappy surrogates are extremely rare. The owner of the surrogacy agency that Priya used told me that Jones’s experience was an “outlier,” one of only three cases out of the hundreds she had overseen that had “gone south.” At the Men Having Babies conference, an agency director assured the attendees that almost all of the “horror stories” reported in the press involved traditional surrogacy, in which the woman carrying the baby uses her own egg. (She added that the traditional approach now accounts for only 5 percent of American surrogacies.) The sales pitch to intended parents for gestational surrogacy—involving an egg from either the commissioning mother or a separate donor—is precisely that the surrogate has no legal claim to custody. That makes it legally safer for the rich couples who pay the bills than a traditional surrogacy. But it may be more physically dangerous for the surrogate. At the Men Having Babies conference, the first audience question was a stark one: How many surrogates die giving birth? Deaths are very rare, Poole-Dayan, the organizer, assured them. A 2020 study found that gestational surrogates were no more likely to die in childbirth than any other pregnant woman. Yet early evidence suggests that carrying a child who is not genetically related to you could increase the risk of complications: A 2024 study of more than 850,000 pregnancies over a decade in Ontario found that “severe maternal morbidity and adverse pregnancy outcomes” were three times higher among gestational carriers than in conventional pregnancies. When the mother and the fetus are not genetically related, the developmental biologist Emma Hilton has written, “Mum’s immune system may ramp up to fight against the wholly foreign tissue. In response, placental invasion becomes more aggressive.” (A systematic review from 2015 found that “most studies reporting on surrogacy have serious methodological limitations.”) Because of the elevated risks associated with twin pregnancies, most reputable agencies now implant only one embryo at a time, but—a recurring theme in this story—no law or professional regulation requires them to do so. To Poole-Dayan, the value of a contract and of compensation is that it forces both parties to have uncomfortable conversations while the risks are still theoretical. “I always tell people, ‘Imagine yourself at the funeral of the surrogate,’ ” he told me. I found Poole-Dayan’s forthrightness a refreshing change from the cloying online culture around surrogacy, with the staged hospital shots and cutesy euphemisms designed to play down the toll of pregnancy and birth. In one video, a little girl born via surrogacy describes the woman who carried her—who built her, cell by cell, inside her own body—as an “Easy-Bake Oven.” When Jones concluded that she had been mistreated, she turned to Kallie Fell. A perinatal nurse by training, Fell works out of an office the size of a janitor’s closet in a co-working space in Pleasant Hill, east of San Francisco. Fell is the executive director of the Center for Bioethics and Culture Network, which was founded in 2000 to campaign against “Big Fertility” but in recent years has also opposed youth gender transition. The CBC has only two full-time employees; Fell told me that it is “lonely work.” Her inbox is full of questions, unhappy stories, and requests for legal help: a surrogate left with medical debt after the intended parents ghosted her, a man who regrets being a sperm donor, women who don’t want to abort a fetus with disabilities but have signed a contract promising to do so. “I’m a little bit of a magnet,” she said. One of the most frequent problems, Fell told me, is the financial imbalance between a surrogate and the intended parents. Ethical agencies will ask the IPs to pay for an independent lawyer to read the contract on their surrogate’s behalf, but no law or regulation enforces this. Contracts therefore tend to be written with the protection of the IPs in mind rather than the carrier. Surrogates can be asked to sign nondisclosure agreements, to protect the privacy of the IPs and the child, but these can also prevent them from speaking honestly about bad experiences. Mental-health troubles can be grounds for disqualification for potential surrogates, but IPs typically face less scrutiny. Last year, Wired reported on a woman with bipolar disorder who blamed her surrogate for having a stillbirth ; in a fury, she sent a photo of the corpse to an iPad belonging to the surrogate’s 7-year-old son. The same imbalance is true of criminal records: Another woman who’d contacted Fell, Amanda Misbahu, told me that midway through her surrogate pregnancy—arranged via Facebook—she began to worry that the IP, a gay single father, hadn’t been entirely honest about his criminal history. To me, Misbahu’s story sounded like a surrogacy nightmare, but she cheerfully insisted that she would be willing to act as a surrogate again. Misbahu’s upbringing had been turbulent. She had been taken away from her own mother when she was six months old, she said, with “maggots in my diapers and Pepsi in my bottles,” and had been raised by a traditionally minded, religious family. The turmoil continued into her adulthood, in successive marriages that didn’t work out. By age 23, Misbahu had given birth to five babies, but none of them lived with her full-time; some were being raised primarily by relatives. Courtney Pedroza for The Atlantic Amanda Misbahu, photographed in Tempe, Arizona. For her, becoming a surrogate was “a way to help me through some of my own trauma.” In her 30s, her thoughts turned to surrogacy. “It was a way for me, in a sentence, to help me through some of my own trauma,” she said. Giving up her own children had left her distraught, she said, yet “with this one, I knew the outcome, I knew it was going to happen, and it was a situation that I knew would be traumatic but I could control.” Two agencies turned her down: the first because of her weight, and the second after her early psychological trauma came up in a medical screening. So she went on Facebook to advertise her services directly to would-be parents. When a man whom I’ll call Cameron got in contact with Misbahu, she wrote her own surrogacy contract, and “he let me pick the egg donor—it was like online dating,” she said. She and Cameron wanted two embryos transferred, but the fertility doctor advised only one. “We said, We’ll take our $100,000 and we’ll go next door ,” she told me. The doctor relented but made her sign a waiver. Only one of the embryos implanted. At eight weeks, she was hospitalized for life-threatening blood clots. She needed blood thinners for the rest of her pregnancy. “I thought she was gonna die,” her fourth child, Alyssa, told me. “So I would just start freaking out randomly when I thought about it—like, at school, sometimes I’d be crying in lunch.” Although Misbahu didn’t know it, Cameron had once pleaded no contest to involuntary manslaughter in California after injecting a friend with a fatal dose of Benadryl in his apartment. He then moved to Kentucky and practiced as a physician’s assistant without a license, a deception that came to light after patients claimed that he had botched their cosmetic surgeries. In 2001, he’d been sentenced to 20 years in prison for five counts of second-degree assault and 112 counts of wanton endangerment, although he was released early. In learning about his past, Misbahu also discovered that he had an adult daughter. In the end, she concluded that he’d turned his life around and that there was nothing she could do except go through with the contract. Cameron and his new boyfriend were present for the birth, for which Misbahu had an epidural for the first time in her history of deliveries, “because I’m like, I don’t want to have to feel any of this ,” she told me. She cried—from the hormones, she recalled—and saw the baby a few hours later: “And I was like, She’s so pretty, but I really just can’t even touch her .” Courtney Pedroza for The Atlantic Misbahu shows a photo of two embryos that she sought to have implanted. Misbahu attended counseling sessions for six months after the birth. “You felt like you lost a baby,” she said. “And I wouldn’t stop pumping milk.” Eventually, a friend told her that she had to move on, and so she donated the breast milk to a local bank for premature babies. Her counselor wasn’t much help, she said: “She thought it was the coolest thing; she had never met a surrogate. She just wanted me to paint pictures in her office. And I was like, Ma’am, I feel like I want to blow out my fucking brains .” Misbahu told me that she even gave her gun to her brother because she was so worried about her mental health. A few months after we first spoke, I met Misbahu in a pancake restaurant on the outskirts of Columbus, Ohio. She turned up bearing a knitted kangaroo that her mother had made for me, and she wore a medical-alert bracelet around her wrist. Her clotting condition had convinced her that she could not advertise herself as a surrogate again. However, she had married a Ghanaian asylum seeker whom she’d met on a dating app, and was trying for a baby with him to strengthen his claim. (They have since split.) For a time, Misbahu had remained in contact with Cameron—and had even helped him find his next surrogate. But eventually, their relationship broke down. She had asked him to buy a present for her daughter, and he’d told her that she couldn’t treat him as an ATM. “Finally, I wrote him back, and I was like, Look, I almost literally died giving birth to your kid. Like, it doesn’t mean you owe me anything. But that was pretty disrespectful ,” she told me. (Cameron did not respond to questions from The Atlantic .) He blocked her on Facebook. But one of her friends could still see his page, so she used that account to secretly watch his daughter—the baby she had carried—grow up. She showed me a photo of the little girl and her siblings on her phone. “The girls are so pretty,” she said with pride. Surrogacy has a supply problem. There are not enough ethically motivated, healthy, middle-class American women to meet demand. Speakers at the Men Having Babies conference repeatedly stressed that reputable agencies accept only 5 percent of applicants as surrogates. Good agencies screen women for health and psychological problems, and question them about their finances and the supportiveness of their partner. Those safeguards are reflected in the high costs. Look abroad, though, and it’s a different story. Some agencies offer “guaranteed baby” packages for as little as $50,000. Surrogacy destinations pop up anywhere the local laws are lax, such as Northern Cyprus, a territory that exists in a legal limbo and is recognized only by Turkey. (The problem is that babies born there can end up stateless.) For parents from Russia, nearby Georgia is a similar no-questions-asked destination. India used to be the most favored low-cost destination, but in 2015, Prime Minister Narendra Modi, citing fears of exploitation, banned commercial surrogacy for foreigners. Ukraine’s appeal as a surrogacy destination has diminished since Russia’s invasion in 2022, although the leading agency there, BioTexCom, told me that the company is still handing off one baby born via surrogacy every day on average, at a cost of about $60,000. A representative of the agency initially told me that it was planning to open a clinic in Kazakhstan, to cater to the growing Asian market. In July, however, that country abruptly banned foreign surrogacy amid concerns about exploitation. BioTexCom takes a more unsentimental approach to surrogacy than American agencies. When I asked Denis Herman, the legal director, what his best day on the job had been, I expected him to tell me about uniting a baby with happy parents. Instead, he talked about business metrics: “I’m really focused on the KPIs, on getting the milestones done.” BioTexCom’s founder, Albert Tochilovsky, told me that he worried about falling birth rates, and presented surrogacy as an alternative to immigration. BioTexCom agreed to let me speak with one of its current surrogates, a 40-year-old whom it identified as Nana, and assigned an employee to translate our conversation. This was Nana’s third surrogate pregnancy since 2021, and she had two much older children of her own. During the first surrogate pregnancy, she was given an apartment to live in with her kids, she told me, so she’d decided to do it twice more; it was her only job. (Compensation for BioTexCom surrogates begins at $23,000, according to the company. The average yearly salary in Ukraine is about $8,700.) The image that Nana and the agency presented was of surrogacy as a sensible economic option and a morally good one. “In Ukraine, we say: Children are a flower of our life,” the translator told me. Mexico is more convenient for Americans, and a journey might cost $100,000 less there than in the States. But babies born in Mexico through surrogacy are given a Mexican passport by default, which can cause problems at the U.S. border. The State Department warns Americans that “there is no legal framework to protect parents who pursue surrogacy in Mexico, despite agencies and clinics promoting Mexico as a safe, legal destination for commercial surrogacy.” Wes Johnson-Ellis of the British firm My Surrogacy Journey has sufficient faith in the Mexican system that he and his husband, Michael, had their third child through a surrogate in Mexico City. Yet he acknowledges the concern that carriers in the country are taking on medical risk out of economic need. “Let’s not be naive,” Johnson-Ellis told me. “In Mexico, the compensation that we offer is three times the average wage, so it is a significant amount of money for them.” He estimated that his team accepts only 20 percent of the women who apply to be surrogates, and he said that they filter out anyone who is motivated only by money. Several surrogacy agencies told me that they worry deeply about the booming market in Mexico, and Johnson-Ellis expressed doubts about his company’s competitors there. “They don’t operate in an ethical way,” he said. “They don’t safeguard everyone; they don’t look after everyone.” Gulati, the practice director of Surrogacy4All, which arranges approximately 200 surrogate pregnancies every year, said that his favored destination for a low-cost journey is now Ghana, where he charges intended parents a flat rate of $49,000. Those carriers are under close watch. “The great thing about doing surrogacy in Ghana is that they live in a dormitory which is right near the hospital, so they can’t drink, they can’t smoke, they can’t do drugs,” he said. “During that period of time, they are monitored 24 hours, seven days a week. And as a result, the success rate with surrogacy is very, very high.” Molly Snee Even in California , the regulation of agencies leaves much to be desired. In May 2025, the caregivers of a two-month-old baby were reported to social services for potential abuse. When the police raided their mansion in Arcadia, a small city northeast of Los Angeles, they discovered another 15 children, who were being homeschooled by a platoon of nannies. “There were probably anywhere from six to eight at the time that we were there,” Captain Kollin Cieadlo of the Arcadia Police Department told me. Footage from surveillance cameras showed that the children were being drilled in English and Mandarin and forced, as a form of discipline, to do squats and other physical exercises that the police considered “above and beyond what a normal punishment would be.” Further searches revealed six more kids whose birth certificates declared them to also be the children of Silvia Zhang and Guojun Xuan , who owned the house. The couple had been running an agency, Mark Surrogacy, with only one client—themselves. In 2023, one of their surrogates had been obligated, thanks to the prebirth order she had signed, to hand over a newly delivered child to people she had never seen before, who arrived at the hospital with power-of-attorney documents. The sheer number of parental orders obtained by Zhang and Xuan during this period triggered an investigation ordered by a judge, but no further action was taken. As news of the mansion raid spread, surrogates then currently under contract with Mark Surrogacy—and still pregnant—began finding one another in Facebook groups. They all told similar stories, of being commissioned by a woman who said that she was unable to conceive and desperately wanted a child. When Zhang and Xuan were questioned by the police, they denied that anything was amiss. “They simply said they just wanted a large family with a lot of kids,” Cieadlo said. The children went into foster care, and one of the surrogates, Kayla Elliott of Corpus Christi, Texas, started a GoFundMe to try to win custody of the child she’d carried. (She has since said that she believes the baby should be left with the foster parents, for continuity of care.) No charges have been filed against Zhang and Xuan, who have since commissioned even more babies. Although they could face police action over the allegations of child abuse, the startling fact is that their baby-creation spree is legal in California. (Their lawyers did not respond to a request for comment.) The Wall Street Journal reported that the police were investigating the couple for possible trafficking, but Zhang told the newspaper that she intended to raise all of the children: “We never sell our babies. We take care of them very well.” After speaking with Jones and Misbahu, I spent hours turning over their stories in my mind, trying to reconcile their bad experiences with the many upbeat counterexamples I had seen at the Men Having Babies conference. None of those women had needed surrogacy to stay solvent, and more than one had joked to me that they could have earned more as an Uber driver. For Veronica Bowers, a two-time surrogate who now works for the Northwest Surrogacy Center in Oregon, surrogacy was a way for her to be with her own kids while still contributing to the household finances. (For similar reasons, military wives are actively recruited by surrogacy agencies.) “It is a badge of honor,” Bowers told me. “I feel really proud that I did this.” The happiest surrogacy experiences I saw resembled open adoptions, where the process is transparent and the birth mother can stay in touch with the child. (Bowers and Roberts are in contact with the children they carried—like an aunt rather than a mother.) The bad stories involved parents who behaved as though they were ordering a baby from a mail-order catalog. I was also left deeply uneasy by the realities of international surrogacy: Why should California be a place where Chinese parents go to find blond, blue-eyed surrogates for status reasons—and why should American parents have the right to acquire a cut-rate child by employing a Ghanaian woman to live in a dormitory under 24/7 monitoring? To protect everyone involved, states should impose upper limits on the age of commissioning parents and on the number of children any couple or individual can commission, as well as an equalization of the disclosure requirements. If surrogates must reveal their medical and criminal histories, then so should the rich people employing them. Something that surprised me was that many of the women I interviewed who had found surrogacy to be a traumatic experience were ambivalent, rather than flatly opposed, to the practice. Jones said that she hadn’t ruled out another journey, although she was still suffering medical complications from the difficult pregnancy and birth. She also worried that the baby girl she had carried would never know “three pertinent people in her life”—the biological father who had died before she was conceived, the egg donor who had provided half of her DNA, and the surrogate who had carried her for nine nausea-filled months. Jones had watched videos online of children born through surrogacy who opposed the practice, and she wondered whether she had been selfless to become a surrogate—or selfish. At the end of our meeting, she said—just as Amanda Misbahu did—that she had carried on pumping breast milk for months after the birth, even though she’d had no baby to nourish. She had also asked friends to check Priya’s social media to see what the baby she’d carried looked like now. On her phone, she showed me a photo of the little girl smiling alongside Priya’s other children. Other than that picture, Jones said, her hospital bracelet and blanket are her only mementos of carrying the girl. She still feels the loss: “Truthfully, even though she’s not my child, she’s my child.” This article appears in the October 2026 print edition with the headline “Mothers for Sale.” When you buy a book using a link on this page, we receive a commission. Thank you for supporting The Atlantic .

items.title: Amrabat–Ouahbi, le divorce est consommé : un départ qui fait débat
items.description: La décision de Sofyan Amrabat de se mettre en retrait de l’équipe nationale marocaine tant que Mohamed Ouahbi restera à la tête des Lions de l’Atlas suscite de nombreuses réactions au Maroc. Si le milieu de terrain de 30 ans assure qu’il ne s’agit pas d’une retraite internationale et réaffirme son attachement au maillot national, une partie des supporters lui reproche la manière choisie pour annoncer son départ. Dans un message publié mardi sur ses réseaux sociaux, Sofyan Amrabat a expliqué qu’il ne se sentait plus en mesure de poursuivre son aventure avec la sélection sous la direction du technicien marocain. Il a toutefois précisé qu’il ne révélait pas les raisons précises de cette décision, préférant les garder privées « par respect pour l’équipe nationale et toutes les personnes concernées ». Le joueur de l’Ajax Amsterdam a également tenu à écarter toute idée de retraite internationale. Il a assuré que la porte restait ouverte à un retour avec les Lions de l’Atlas à l’avenir et a adressé ses vœux de réussite à ses coéquipiers ainsi qu’au staff technique. Une décision qui passe mal auprès d’une partie des supporters Malgré ce discours, l’annonce a rapidement provoqué une vague de critiques sur les réseaux sociaux. Plusieurs supporters estiment qu’Amrabat aurait dû accepter la concurrence et respecter les choix du sélectionneur, plutôt que de conditionner sa présence avec la sélection au départ de Mohamed Ouahbi. Sur les réseaux sociaux, certains internautes lui reprochent notamment de ne pas accepter son nouveau statut au sein du groupe. La montée en puissance de jeunes milieux de terrain comme Ayoub Bouaddi et Neil El Aynaoui a progressivement réduit son temps de jeu, notamment lors de la Coupe du monde 2026. Plusieurs commentaires considèrent ainsi que le joueur aurait dû privilégier l’intérêt collectif plutôt que d’exposer publiquement son différend avec le sélectionneur, rappelant ainsi que personne n'est au-dessus de la sélection. 𝗧𝗢𝗨𝗧 𝗡𝗢𝗧𝗥𝗘 𝗦𝗢𝗨𝗧𝗜𝗘𝗡 à Mohamed Ouahbi ! Personne n’est au-dessus de la sélection. Si Sofyan Amrabat refuse de continuer avec le sélectionneur, alors bonne continuation à lui. pic.twitter.com/gx7ozSoJl2 — FRMF Xtra (@FRMFXtra) September 8, 2026 Sofyan Amrabat espérait sans doute susciter de l’empathie auprès des Marocains après sa décision. Mais c’est tout l’inverse qui s’est produit : unanimement, les marocains ont affiché leur soutien à Mohamed Ouahbi. Il faut se rendre à l’évidence : l’histoire d’Amrabat avec la… pic.twitter.com/8kJrwEsA9j — KoraMaroc (@AtKoraMaroc) September 8, 2026 Sofyan Amrabat n’a pas apprécié son passage sur le banc, mais le message du sélectionneur est 𝗖𝗟𝗔𝗜𝗥. 𝐀𝐮𝐜𝐮𝐧𝐞 𝐩𝐥𝐚𝐜𝐞 𝐧’𝐞𝐬𝐭 𝐠𝐚𝐫𝐚𝐧𝐭𝐢𝐞. Tu performes, tu joues. Tu ne performes plus, ta place est en jeu. pic.twitter.com/PhB86TOpVM — FRMF Xtra (@FRMFXtra) September 8, 2026 [ MAROC | LIONS DE L’ATLAS ] SOFYAN AMRABAt L'ULTIMATUM Amrabat refuse de jouer sous les ordres de Mohamed Ouahbi. Il se met en retrait tant que le sélectionneur reste. Un ultimatum. Dommage de finir sa carrière avec les Lions en mode gamin capricieux Merci pour… pic.twitter.com/VrcTY3jsAh — MD (@GeoCherifien) September 9, 2026 D’autres voix se montrent toutefois plus mesurées et rappellent qu’Amrabat n’a jamais affirmé publiquement qu’il refusait la concurrence ou qu’il exigeait une place de titulaire. Le principal intéressé n’ayant pas dévoilé les raisons de son choix, toute interprétation sur ses motivations demeure donc spéculative. 1- Parler d’« égo » sur la base de « sources anonymes », c'est de la rumeur, pas de l'analyse. Partout en Europe, Amrabat a été salué pour son éthique irréprochable. Un cadre de son vécu qui exprime un désaccord ne fait pas un caprice : il défend une exigence sportive et c'est… https://t.co/yoUZXvW2BC pic.twitter.com/ueCikmEDVZ — Yahia (@SeulementCtyen) September 8, 2026 Rp honnête on n'aime pas tous Amrabat mais il a du se passer qlq chose en coulisse il est pas du genre à faire une decla comme sa a voir https://t.co/kt9IT5mtEH — (@Jongaly07) September 8, 2026 The reason is he don't want to be in the bench, that easy. Thank you for 2022 but time to move on from Amrabat, We have Bouaddi, El Aynaoui, El Mourabet, El Faouzi, Richardson, Belahyane and more https://t.co/Ga0Brt1Sxd — FWC30 (@FWC30_Central) September 8, 2026 Des tensions déjà apparues après le Mondial Cette annonce ne tombe pas totalement de nulle part. Après l’élimination du Maroc en quarts de finale de la Coupe du monde 2026 face à la France, le frère de Sofyan Amrabat, Mohamed Amrabat, avait publiquement évoqué la frustration du milieu de terrain et ses relations difficiles avec Mohamed Ouahbi. Il avait notamment affirmé que son frère en avait « complètement assez de cet entraîneur ». Quelques jours plus tard, Ouahbi avait répondu à ces polémiques en affirmant qu’il n’existait pas de véritable conflit avec son joueur et que la frustration d’Amrabat était principalement liée à son temps de jeu. Le sélectionneur avait également souligné que le milieu de terrain possédait une forte personnalité et qu’il aurait pu venir lui parler directement s’il rencontrait un problème avec lui. D’un cadre incontournable à un rôle secondaire Le contexte sportif explique en partie l’ampleur de la polémique. Figure majeure de la sélection marocaine lors de l’épopée historique de la Coupe du monde 2022, Amrabat n’a plus le même statut depuis l’arrivée de Mohamed Ouahbi. Lors du Mondial 2026, le joueur n’a débuté qu'une seule rencontre et a dû composer avec une concurrence accrue dans l’entrejeu. L’émergence d’Ayoub Bouaddi, mais aussi les prestations de Neil El Aynaoui, ont contribué à modifier la hiérarchie au milieu de terrain. C’est précisément cette évolution qui alimente une partie des critiques : certains supporters estiment qu’Amrabat, désormais âgé de 30 ans, doit accepter la nouvelle concurrence et accompagner la transition générationnelle plutôt que de se retirer en réaction à la diminution de son rôle. Une rupture, mais pas un adieu définitif Pour autant, Sofyan Amrabat n’a pas fermé définitivement la porte à la sélection. Son message insiste au contraire sur son amour pour le Maroc et sur son soutien aux Lions de l’Atlas. Il affirme vouloir continuer à suivre l’équipe et à la soutenir, même depuis les tribunes. Son retrait apparaît donc comme une décision conditionnée au maintien de Mohamed Ouahbi, plutôt que comme une rupture définitive avec la sélection. Une situation qui place désormais le milieu de terrain et le sélectionneur au centre d’une polémique appelée à se poursuivre, alors que les Lions de l’Atlas doivent entamer prochainement leur campagne de qualification pour la CAN 2027. Le Maroc doit affronter le Gabon le 25 septembre avant de défier le Lesotho quatre jours plus tard. Amrabat, lui, observera ces échéances depuis l’extérieur, avec une question qui restera en suspens : son retrait constitue-t-il une simple parenthèse ou le début de la fin de son aventure internationale avec les Lions de l’Atlas ? items.title: 7-Octobre : Netanyahou aurait été personnellement averti avant l'attaque
items.description: De nouvelles revelations relancent la controverse sur les responsabilites israeliennes avant l'attaque du Hamas du 7 octobre 2023. Selon une enquete publiee par Haaretz, Benjamin Netanyahou aurait recu, une dizaine de jours avant l'assaut, un avertissement direct du president emirati Mohammed ben Zayed sur la preparation d'une operation majeure depuis Gaza. L'information provient d'un livre a paraître des journalistes Shlomi Eldar et Ruth Yuval, fonde sur des dizaines d'entretiens avec des responsables israeliens et etrangers. Selon leur recit, MBZ aurait echange pendant environ 45 minutes avec Netanyahou fin septembre 2023. Il l'aurait prevenu que Yahya Sinwar preparait une attaque susceptible de provoquer un important bain de sang et de destabiliser toute la region. Une mauvaise nouvelle avant les elections Le Premier ministre israelien aurait neanmoins reagi avec calme, assurant qu'Israel etait prepare a differents scenarios et estimant qu'une menace plus serieuse pouvait venir de Cisjordanie. Surtout, selon Haaretz, cette mise en garde n'aurait pas ete transmise aux principaux responsables securitaires israeliens. Le bureau de Netanyahou rejette categoriquement ces affirmations, parlant d'un « mensonge absolu » et niant qu'un tel echange ait ete recu. Mais une source emiratie a confirme au Times of Israel que MBZ avait bien prevenu le chef du gouvernement israelien d'un projet d'attaque du Hamas. Ces revelations sont particulierement explosives alors qu'Israel s'approche des elections du 27 octobre et que Netanyahou continue de s'opposer a la creation d'une commission d'enquete independante sur les defaillances ayant precede le 7-Octobre. Plusieurs figures de l'opposition l'accusent desormais d'avoir ignore un avertissement majeur et reclament qu'il rende des comptes. Elles ne prouvent pas que Netanyahou connaissait precisement la date ou le deroulement de l'attaque. Elles renforcent en revanche les questions sur les signaux d'alerte recus par le pouvoir israelien avant le 7 octobre et sur les raisons pour lesquelles ils n'ont pas conduit a une mobilisation securitaire.

items.title: Weija Dam: GWL says plans are in place to desilt reservoir when necessary
items.description: Ghana Water Limited (GWL) says the Weija Dam currently has sufficient capacity to supply water to the western part of Accra throughout the year, but plans are in place to desilt the reservoir when necessary. Head of Public Relations and Communications at GWL, Stanley Martey, said regular desilting of rivers and reservoirs is important to maintain adequate water levels for treatment and supply. Speaking on Joy FM’s Super Morning Show on Wednesday, September 9, in a discussion on the Weija Dam spillage, Mr Martey was asked about concerns over possible siltation of the reservoir and what the company was doing to address the issue. He said the current dam remains adequate for the area it serves. “With the dam for now, I think it is enough to save the western part of Accra throughout the year without any challenge,” he said. Mr Martey, however, acknowledged that siltation is an issue that has to be addressed over time. “Be that as it may, we still have to desilt when it is silted. And there are plans to do that,” he said. He explained that desilting is not something that needs to be done continuously, but is carried out periodically when required. “Beyond some of these rivers, and especially what we do almost every 15, 20 years, there should be some desilting,” he said. “And which we will do when the time is up.” According to Mr Martey, the need to maintain the capacity of water bodies is particularly important because the water stored in the reservoir is ultimately treated for public consumption. He said GWL has procedures in place to ensure that its water sources are properly managed. “As for desilting of river bodies and dams, especially for what we have, because we have to transfer the treatment and for consumption, we need to ensure that we always have enough water within the reservoir to feed us throughout the year,” he said. Mr Martey said the company follows established procedures to ensure that the reservoir continues to provide sufficient raw water for treatment. “So, Ghana Water Company, we follow our standard operating procedures to ensure that these things are done,” he said.

items.title: Weija Dam spillage necessary to prevent dam collapse – GWL
items.description: Ghana Water Limited (GWL) says the release of excess water from the Weija Dam is necessary to protect the structure from potential collapse, despite the flooding and damage to properties it may cause in surrounding communities. The Head of Public Relations and Communications at GWL, Stanley Martey, described the impact of the current spillage on residents as “disheartening” but said allowing water levels to rise beyond safe limits could result in a far greater disaster. Speaking on the Joy FM Super Morning Show on Wednesday, September 9 , Mr Martey explained that dams are designed with spill gates to allow operators to release excess water when levels become difficult to manage. “There’ll be a point in time when the levels will go beyond a certain manageable level, and so we have to open the steel gate for the excess water to flow,” he said. Risk of dam collapse Mr Martey said the controlled release is also intended to protect the structural integrity of the Weija Dam, warning that excessive water pressure could weaken the structure and eventually cause it to fail. He said a breach in the dam could start small but gradually expand into a major collapse. “If a pinhole is created within these stones, it will enlarge, and one day it will just collapse,” he said. According to him, such a collapse could lead to significantly greater loss of lives and property than the flooding currently being experienced along the Densu River. He added that a collapse would also disrupt water supply to large parts of western Accra because GWL relies on the dam as a source of raw water for treatment. “Until the dam is rebuilt, Ghana Water wouldn’t be able to extract water for treatment,” he said, warning that rebuilding a dam could take three years or more. Encroachment worsening flood impact Mr Martey attributed part of the damage caused by rising water levels to encroachment on river buffer zones. He explained that rivers naturally follow their courses and that regulations provide for buffer zones along waterways to allow water to flow without threatening buildings and other structures. However, he said some people have occupied and built on these areas, with others allegedly filling parts of river channels. “People have encroached on the buffer zone to the extent that they’re even filling the river and putting up structures,” he said. He said blocking the natural path of water forces it to seek alternative routes, increasing the risk of flooding. Mr Martey therefore called on district assemblies to strictly enforce regulations governing development along river courses and prevent construction in unauthorised areas. He also urged residents to exercise greater caution when purchasing land and constructing properties, particularly in known flood-prone areas. Spill gates serve several purposes Beyond managing excess water, Mr Martey said spill gates can also help improve water quality by allowing turbid water to flow out before fresh inflows enter the dam. He maintained that controlled releases are a normal part of dam operations and are preferable to allowing water levels to reach a point where the structure could be compromised. “There are reasons behind the construction of a dam, and then the addition of spill gates. These things are bound to happen,” he said. Mr Martey acknowledged the hardship caused by the current spillage but maintained that releasing excess water remains necessary to protect the dam and prevent a potentially catastrophic failure. “There’s nothing we can do other than spill the excess water and avoid the collapse of the dam,” he said.

items.title: Festival SICA 2026 : Foudis Diallo, la « Reine du Blues pastoral », porte les couleurs de la Guinée
items.description: La chanteuse guinéenne Foudis Diallo, affectueusement surnommée la « Reine du Blues pastoral », s’apprête à défendre les couleurs de la Guinée au Festival SICA 2026, au Bénin. L’artiste est nominée dans la catégorie « Music Afro-Ethnic » de cette compétition internationale, qui se tiendra du 9 au 15 novembre 2026. Cette nomination vient mettre en lumière le parcours de Foudis Diallo ainsi que son univers musical, marqué par les sonorités pastorales. À travers sa participation, la chanteuse entend faire découvrir au public international une autre facette de la richesse culturelle et musicale guinéenne. Face à des artistes venus de différents horizons, Foudis Diallo aura l’occasion de promouvoir son identité artistique et de porter haut les couleurs de son pays sur une scène dédiée à la création musicale africaine. Avec cette participation au Festival SICA 2026, la « Reine du Blues pastoral » ambitionne ainsi de faire voyager les sonorités guinéennes au-delà des frontières et de contribuer au rayonnement de la musique nationale sur la scène africaine. items.title: Attaque nocturne de drones ukrainiens : quatre morts, dont un enfant, et 29 blessés à Novorossiïsk
items.description: Le kraï de Krasnodar a ete vise dans la nuit du 8 au 9 septembre par une attaque massive de drones ukrainiens. Novorossiïsk, importante ville portuaire russe situee sur la mer Noire, a ete la plus durement touchee. Le gouverneur regional, Veniamine Kondratiev, a fait etat de quatre morts, dont un enfant, et de 29 blesses. La defense antiaerienne russe a ete mobilisee durant la nuit face aux drones detectes au-dessus de la region, tandis que les services d'urgence intervenaient sur les differents sites touches. Le ministere russe de la Sante a ensuite precise la situation des blesses. Alexeï Kouznetsov, assistant du ministre, a indique que 28 personnes, dont deux enfants, avaient ete hospitalisees a Novorossiïsk. Une autre victime a recu des soins sans hospitalisation. Selon un point de situation du ministere, un patient se trouvait alors dans un etat grave, les autres etant dans un etat de gravite moyenne. Des specialistes du Centre federal de medecine de catastrophe ont egalement ete mobilises en soutien aux equipes medicales locales. Des habitations et des bâtiments civils endommages Les degâts recenses a Novorossiïsk concernent plusieurs secteurs civils de la ville. Trois maisons individuelles, cinq immeubles d'habitation, un jardin d'enfants ainsi qu'une eglise orthodoxe ont ete endommages. La polyclinique numero 2 a elle aussi subi d'importants degâts et a temporairement suspendu l'accueil des patients. Le gouverneur Veniamine Kondratiev a affirme que les forces ukrainiennes avaient frappe « exclusivement des objectifs civils » et a demande aux autorites municipales d'evaluer rapidement les dommages et d'apporter une aide aux familles concernees. D'autres consequences ont ete recensees dans la matinee. Trois entreprises ont ete touchees, selon le maire Andreï Kravtchenko. Une conduite d'eau de la rue Magistralnaïa et les installations electriques du reseau de trolleybus ont egalement ete endommagees, entraînant des perturbations dans le secteur. Un regime d'etat d'urgence a par ailleurs ete instaure a Novorossiïsk. Les consequences de l'attaque ont egalement ete constatees a Anapa. Des debris de drones ont endommage plusieurs habitations, des vehicules, des bâtiments d'entreprises et le jardin d'enfants « Volna ». Aucune victime n'y a ete signalee. La chute de debris a egalement provoque un incendie dans une zone forestiere de la reserve naturelle d'Outrich. La defense antiaerienne mobilisee dans plusieurs regions russes Gelendjik a egalement ete visee au cours de la nuit. Le maire Alexeï Bogodistov a decrit cette nuit comme la plus inquietante pour la ville. De nombreux drones ont ete detectes et pris pour cible tout au long de la nuit par les systemes de defense antiaerienne et des groupes mobiles. Selon lui, « les objectifs de l'adversaire n'ont pas ete atteints ». L'attaque s'est etendue bien au-dela du seul kraï de Krasnodar. Selon le ministere russe de la Defense, les forces de defense antiaerienne ont intercepte et detruit 596 drones ukrainiens entre 20 heures le 8 septembre et 8 heures le lendemain. Les appareils ont ete neutralises au-dessus de plusieurs regions russes, dont le kraï de Krasnodar et la Crimee, ainsi qu'au-dessus de la mer Noire Apres l'attaque contre Novorossiïsk, le Comite d'enquete russe a ouvert une procedure penale pour acte terroriste.
